board_events.text: Root system: descending, develops from the radicle, usually non-green.
Root jobs: absorb water and minerals, anchor the plant, store food, make plant-growth regulators.
Shoot system: ascending, develops from the plumule. Stem, leaves, buds, later flowers and fruits.
Shoot jobs: manufacture food, store it, and eventually handle reproduction.
Root system + shoot system = the plant body axis.
Every organ in this chapter is one of these two departments doing an unusual job.

segments.text: <curious>Picture a flowering plant the way you would picture a small family business that runs exactly two departments.
One department works underground, out of sight, fetching raw materials and keeping the whole thing anchored. The other works above ground, in the open.
The underground department is the root system. It is the descending part of the plant, it develops from the radicle, and it is usually not green.
Its jobs are practical ones. It absorbs water and minerals from the soil, it anchors the plant, it can store food, and it even makes plant-growth regulators.
The above-ground department is the shoot system. It develops from the plumule, and it is built from the stem, the leaves, the buds, and later the flowers and fruits.
Its jobs are manufacturing, storage, and eventually reproduction. This is where photosynthesis runs and where the next generation gets launched.
Put the two together and you have the plant body axis. That single phrase covers every organ we will study in this subtopic.
And here is the promise of the whole topic. Every strange organ you will meet, a thorn, a tendril, a potato, is only one of these two departments doing an unusual job.
<curious>Ek flowering plant को ऐसे सोचिए जैसे कोई छोटा family business हो, जिसमें ठीक दो departments हैं।
Ek department ज़मीन के नीचे काम करता है, raw materials लाता है और पूरे plant को anchor करके रखता है। दूसरा ऊपर, खुली हवा में।
नीचे वाला department है root system। ये plant का descending हिस्सा है, radicle से develop होता है, और आम तौर पर green नहीं होता।
इसके काम बिल्कुल practical हैं। ये soil से water और minerals absorb करता है, plant को anchor करता है, food store कर सकता है, और plant-growth regulators भी बनाता है।
ऊपर वाला department है shoot system। ये plumule से develop होता है, और इसमें आते हैं stem, leaves, buds, और बाद में flowers और fruits।
इसका काम है manufacturing, storage, और आख़िर में reproduction। यहीं photosynthesis चलता है और यहीं से अगली generation शुरू होती है।
दोनों को मिला दीजिए तो बनता है plant का body axis। यही एक phrase इस पूरे subtopic के हर organ को cover कर लेता है।
और यही इस topic का वादा है। जो भी अजीब organ आपको मिलेगा — thorn, tendril, potato — वो इन्हीं दो departments में से किसी एक का unusual काम है।

board_events.text: Direction: root descends into the soil; stem ascends into the air.
Colour: root usually non-green; stem green when young, woody and brown later.
A root has NO nodes, NO internodes, NO leaves, and NO buds.
A stem HAS nodes and internodes, and carries buds: terminal at the tip, axillary in the leaf axil.
Hairs: root hairs are unicellular. Origin: root from the radicle, stem from the plumule.
Almost every trick question in this subtopic is built on confusing these two.

segments.text: The single most useful idea in this whole subtopic is the difference between a root and a stem, because almost every trick question is built on confusing the two.
Look at the checklist on the board, because this is the list you will actually run in the exam hall, feature by feature.
Start with direction. A root is the descending part. It grows down into the soil. A stem is the opposite. It grows up, into the air and the light.
Colour next. A root is usually non-green, because it lives in the dark and has no reason to photosynthesise. A stem is green when young, and turns woody and brown as it ages.
Now the decisive line, and I want you to hold this one hard. A root has no nodes, no internodes, no leaves, and no buds. Not a single one of the four.
A stem is the exact opposite on every count. It bears nodes and internodes, and it carries buds: a terminal bud at the tip, and axillary buds in the angle where a leaf meets the stem.
Two smaller features finish the list. Root hairs are unicellular, single-celled outgrowths. And the origin differs: a root comes from the radicle, a stem comes from the plumule.
<whisper>Notice what is not on this list: where the organ sits. Depth in the soil never decides anything. Features decide, and only features.
इस पूरे subtopic का सबसे useful idea है root और stem का फ़र्क़, क्योंकि यहाँ का लगभग हर trick question इन्हीं दोनों को confuse कराने पर बना होता है।
Board पर दी हुई checklist देखिए, क्योंकि exam hall में आप असल में यही list feature by feature चलाएँगे।
पहले direction। Root descending हिस्सा है, ये soil में नीचे की ओर बढ़ता है। Stem बिल्कुल उल्टा — ये ऊपर, hava और light की तरफ़ बढ़ता है।
अब colour। Root आम तौर पर non-green होता है, क्योंकि वो अंधेरे में रहता है और उसे photosynthesise करने की ज़रूरत ही नहीं। Stem जब young होता है तो green, और उम्र के साथ woody और brown।
अब वो decisive line, जिसे मैं चाहती हूँ आप पक्का पकड़ लें। Root में कोई nodes नहीं, कोई internodes नहीं, कोई leaves नहीं, और कोई buds नहीं। चारों में से एक भी नहीं।
Stem हर point पर उल्टा है। उसमें nodes और internodes होते हैं, और buds भी — tip पर terminal bud, और leaf जहाँ stem से मिलती है उस angle में axillary bud।
दो छोटे features list पूरी कर देते हैं। Root hairs unicellular होते हैं, यानी single-celled। और origin अलग है — root radicle से, stem plumule से।
<whisper>ध्यान दीजिए कि इस list में क्या नहीं है — organ कहाँ बैठा है, ये। Soil में depth कभी कुछ decide नहीं करती। Features decide करते हैं, सिर्फ़ features।

board_events.text: Node: the point on a stem from which a leaf, or a whorl of leaves, arises.
Internode: the region of stem between two successive nodes.
Bud: a compact, undeveloped shoot. Terminal at the apex; axillary in the axil of a leaf.
A leaf can only board at a station: a leaf always arises at a node.
A root has no railway line at all: no stations, no fixed boarding points.
So potato eyes are buds at nodes: a stem. The sweet potato has none: a root.

segments.text: Think about it this way. The stem is a railway line, and the nodes are the stations along it.
Look at the board. A leaf can only board the train at a station, which is the biological statement that a leaf always arises at a node.
So let us name the parts properly. A node is the point on a stem from which a leaf, or a whorl of leaves, arises. It is a position, not a lump.
The stretch of empty track between two stations is the internode: the region of stem between two successive nodes.
And a bud is a compact, undeveloped shoot, a shoot waiting its turn. A terminal bud sits at the apex. An axillary bud sits in the axil of a leaf.
Now here is why the analogy earns its keep. A root has no railway line at all. No stations, no internode stretches, no fixed boarding points anywhere along it.
That is exactly why absence of nodes and internodes is the textbook way to tell a root from an underground stem.

<chuckle>So dig up a potato and a sweet potato. The potato has tiny eyes, buds sitting at nodes, so it is a stem. The sweet potato is a swollen root with no such buds. Same basket, completely different organs.
इसे ऐसे सोचिए। Stem एक railway line है, और nodes उस line के stations हैं।
Board देखिए। Leaf सिर्फ़ station पर ही train पकड़ सकती है — biology की भाषा में, leaf हमेशा node पर ही arise करती है।
तो parts को ठीक से नाम दे देते हैं। Node वो point है stem पर जहाँ से leaf, या leaves का whorl निकलता है। ये एक position है, कोई गाँठ नहीं।
दो stations के बीच की ख़ाली पटरी है internode — यानी दो successive nodes के बीच का stem का region।
और bud है एक compact, undeveloped shoot — अपनी बारी का इंतज़ार करता shoot। Terminal bud apex पर बैठता है, axillary bud leaf के axil में।
अब असली फ़ायदा यहाँ है। Root में तो railway line है ही नहीं। न stations, न internode की stretches, कहीं भी कोई fixed boarding point नहीं।
इसीलिए nodes और internodes की absence ही textbook तरीक़ा है root को underground stem से अलग पहचानने का।
<chuckle>तो एक potato और एक sweet potato खोदिए। Potato पर छोटी-छोटी eyes हैं, यानी nodes पर बैठे buds — मतलब stem। Sweet potato एक swollen root है, ऐसा कोई bud नहीं। Basket एक, organs बिल्कुल अलग।

board_events.text: The leaf is a flat green outgrowth that arises at a node.
Its headline job: photosynthesis. It is the plant's kitchen, its food factory.
A leaf almost always carries a bud in its axil.
Flatness is not an accident: maximum sunlight intercepted per gram of tissue.
Like a shopkeeper spreading goods across a counter, not piling them in a column.
The leaf is the third member of the trio: root, stem, leaf.

segments.text: The leaf is the third member of the trio, after root and stem, and unlike them it has just one headline job.
Look at the board. That job is photosynthesis. The leaf is the plant's kitchen, its food factory, and almost everything about its shape follows from that.
Structurally, the leaf is a flat green outgrowth that arises at a node. Both halves of that sentence matter: flat and green, and at a node.
And it almost always carries a bud in its axil. Remember that detail, because later in this subtopic it becomes the test that settles a whole class of questions.
Now, why flat? Flatness is not an accident. A leaf is flat so that it can intercept the maximum sunlight per gram of tissue it invests.
Look at the two shapes on the board. Spread the same tissue into a thin sheet and every gram is in the light. Pile it into a block and only the top layer earns anything.
It is the same reason a shopkeeper spreads goods across a wide counter rather than piling them in a column. Surface facing the customer is what pays.
So the trio is complete. The root fetches, the stem carries and connects, and the leaf manufactures. Everything else in this subtopic is one of these three, modified.
Leaf इस trio का तीसरा member है, root और stem के बाद, और इन दोनों के उलट इसका सिर्फ़ एक headline job है।
Board देखिए। वो job है photosynthesis। Leaf plant की kitchen है, उसकी food factory, और इसकी shape की लगभग हर बात इसी से निकलती है।
Structure के हिसाब से leaf एक flat green outgrowth है जो node पर arise करती है। इस sentence के दोनों हिस्से important हैं — flat और green, और node पर।
और इसके axil में लगभग हमेशा एक bud होता है। ये detail याद रखिए, क्योंकि आगे यही एक पूरी class के questions का faisla कर देगा।
अब सवाल — flat क्यों? Flatness कोई accident नहीं है। Leaf इसलिए flat है ताकि जितना tissue लगाया है, उसके हर gram पर maximum sunlight पड़े।
Board पर दोनों shapes देखिए। वही tissue अगर पतली sheet में फैला दें तो हर gram light में है। उसी को block में ढेर कर दें तो सिर्फ़ ऊपर वाली layer कमाती है।
यही वजह है कि दुकानदार सामान चौड़े counter पर फैलाता है, column में ढेर नहीं लगाता। जो surface customer की तरफ़ है, वही कमाता है।
तो trio पूरा हुआ। Root लाता है, stem carry और connect करता है, leaf manufacture करती है। इस subtopic में बाक़ी सब इन्हीं तीन का modified रूप है।

board_events.text: Morphology: external form and arrangement of organs, seen with the naked eye.
Anatomy: internal tissues seen under a microscope. A different chapter.
Trigger words: transverse section, pericycle, casparian strips, vascular bundles.
Trap two: 'underground means root' is wrong. Ginger, turmeric and potato are underground stems.
Trap three: the root-versus-stem rules hold for the typical case.
Some adventitious roots arise from stem nodes. Reason from defining features, not from position.

segments.text: Before we go further, three limits on everything you are about to learn. Miss these and you will lose marks you had already earned.
Look at the board. This subtopic is about external morphology: the form and arrangement of organs you can see with the naked eye.
It is not anatomy. Anatomy deals with internal tissues, the epidermis, the cortex, the vascular bundles, seen under a microscope. Mixing the two is the commonest conceptual error here.

So keep a trigger list. If a question mentions a transverse section, or the pericycle, or casparian strips, or vascular bundles, it has left morphology and entered anatomy. The answer lives in a different chapter.
The second limit is a shortcut that feels right and is wrong. Underground equals root. It does not. Ginger, turmeric, and potato are all underground stems.
They are stems because they carry nodes, scale-leaves, and buds. Depth in the soil is not a defining feature of anything, and examiners know exactly how tempting it is.
The third limit is subtler. The root-versus-stem rules hold for the typical case, but nature keeps exceptions in its pocket. Some adventitious roots arise from stem nodes.
So the standing instruction for this whole subtopic is this: always reason from the defining features, never from where the organ happens to sit.
आगे बढ़ने से पहले तीन limits, जो आप जो सीखने वाले हैं उस पूरे पर लगती हैं। ये चूक गए तो कमाए हुए marks भी चले जाएँगे।
Board देखिए। ये subtopic external morphology के बारे में है — organs की वो form और arrangement जो naked eye से दिखती है।
ये anatomy नहीं है। Anatomy internal tissues देखती है — epidermis, cortex, vascular bundles — microscope के नीचे। इन दोनों को मिला देना यहाँ की सबसे common conceptual ग़लती है।
तो एक trigger list रखिए। अगर question में transverse section आए, या pericycle, या casparian strips, या vascular bundles — तो वो morphology छोड़कर anatomy में जा चुका है। जवाब दूसरे chapter में है।
दूसरी limit एक ऐसा shortcut है जो सही लगता है पर है ग़लत — underground यानी root। नहीं। Ginger, turmeric, और potato — तीनों underground stems हैं।
ये stems इसलिए हैं क्योंकि इनमें nodes, scale-leaves और buds होते हैं। Soil में depth किसी चीज़ का defining feature नहीं है, और examiners को पता है ये कितना tempting है।
तीसरी limit थोड़ी subtle है। Root-versus-stem के rules typical case के लिए हैं, पर nature अपनी जेब में exceptions रखती है। कुछ adventitious roots stem के nodes से निकलती हैं।
तो इस पूरे subtopic का standing instruction यही है — हमेशा defining features से reason कीजिए, कभी इस बात से नहीं कि organ बैठा कहाँ है।

board_events.text: Tap root: from the radicle. One main root with laterals. Most dicots. Example: mustard.
Fibrous: many fine roots from the stem base; the primary root is short-lived. Most monocots. Example: wheat.
Adventitious: from any part other than the radicle. Examples: grass, banyan, Monstera, maize.
The classifier is ORIGIN, not shape: radicle, or not from the radicle.
Tap goes with dicot; fibrous goes with monocot. Store the pair with its example.
Adventitious is defined negatively, which is why it spans such varied plants.

segments.text: Now that a root is properly defined, we can sort root systems into three types. Look at the board, and read them left to right.
A tap root system develops from the radicle. One main root drives down and throws out laterals along its length. This is the pattern of most dicots, and the standard example is mustard.

A fibrous root system is a very different picture. Many fine roots arise from the base of the stem, and the primary root is short-lived. This is the pattern of most monocots, and the standard example is wheat.
Adventitious roots are the third type: roots arising from any part other than the radicle. The plants are varied, and the examples are grass, banyan, Monstera, and maize.
Now catch the logic underneath. The classifier here is origin, not appearance. Ask where the root came from: the radicle, or somewhere else entirely.
That is also why tap and fibrous read as opposites. Tap keeps the radicle and builds on it. Fibrous lets the radicle go and grows its roots from the stem base instead.
Tie each type to its group and its example in one breath: tap goes with dicot goes with mustard; fibrous goes with monocot goes with wheat. Store the triplet, not the lone word.
<excited>And notice that adventitious is defined negatively, by what it is not. Not from the radicle. That is exactly why it can span a grass, a banyan tree, and a maize plant without contradiction.
अब जब root ठीक से define हो गया है, हम root systems को तीन types में बाँट सकते हैं। Board देखिए, बाएँ से दाएँ पढ़िए।
Tap root system radicle से develop होता है। एक main root नीचे जाता है और अपनी लंबाई भर laterals निकालता है। ये ज़्यादातर dicots का pattern है, और standard example है mustard।
Fibrous root system तस्वीर ही बदल देता है। बहुत सारी fine roots stem के base से निकलती हैं, और primary root short-lived होता है। ये ज़्यादातर monocots का pattern है, standard example है wheat।
तीसरा type है adventitious — यानी वो roots जो radicle के अलावा किसी भी हिस्से से निकलें। Plants varied हैं, और examples हैं grass, banyan, Monstera, और maize।
अब नीचे की logic पकड़िए। यहाँ classifier है origin, appearance नहीं। सवाल यही है — root आया कहाँ से, radicle से या कहीं और से।
इसीलिए tap और fibrous उल्टे लगते हैं। Tap radicle को रखता है और उसी पर build करता है। Fibrous radicle को जाने देता है और roots stem base से उगा लेता है।
हर type को उसके group और example के साथ एक साँस में बाँधिए — tap यानी dicot यानी mustard; fibrous यानी monocot यानी wheat। अकेला शब्द नहीं, पूरा triplet store कीजिए।

<excited>और ध्यान दीजिए, adventitious negatively define हुआ है — इस बात से कि वो क्या नहीं है। Radicle से नहीं। इसीलिए इसमें एक grass, एक banyan tree, और एक maize plant, तीनों बिना contradiction के आ जाते हैं।

board_events.text: Root cap: a thimble of cells protecting the delicate apex as the root forces through soil.
Meristematic zone: small, thin-walled, rapidly dividing cells. The engine room supplying new cells.
Zone of elongation: the new cells stretch lengthwise. This is what drives the root down.
Zone of maturation: cells differentiate; the epidermis throws out root hairs.
Root hairs are confined here and do the actual water and mineral absorption. Lateral roots also originate here.
Division first, elongation pushes, maturation works: absorption is behind the tip, never at it.

segments.text: Now zoom right into the growing tip of a root, because the exam loves this sequence. Reasoning from tip to base, in growth order, there are four zones.
The very tip is covered by the root cap, a thimble of cells that protects the delicate apex as the root forces its way through soil. It is armour, and it is sacrificial.
Just behind it is the meristematic zone, packed with small, thin-walled, rapidly dividing cells. This is the engine room. Every cell the root will ever use is made here.
The new cells are then pushed into the zone of elongation, where they stretch lengthwise. Look at the board. This stretching is what actually drives the root down through the soil.
Finally comes the zone of maturation, where cells differentiate into their final forms and the epidermis throws out root hairs.
That makes this band the working zone. Root hairs are confined to the zone of maturation and do the actual water and mineral absorption. Lateral roots also originate here.
Now hold the logic, because the logic is the answer to half the questions. Division happens first, elongation pushes, maturation works.
<whisper>Which means absorption is a little behind the tip, never at the very tip. If an option puts root hairs at the apex, it is wrong before you finish reading it.
अब root के growing tip में बिल्कुल zoom कीजिए, क्योंकि exam को ये sequence बहुत पसंद है। Tip से base तक, growth order में, चार zones हैं।
सबसे tip पर होता है root cap — cells की एक thimble जो delicate apex को बचाती है जब root soil को चीरकर आगे बढ़ता है। ये armour है, और ये घिसने के लिए ही है।
उसके ठीक पीछे है meristematic zone, जो छोटे, thin-walled, तेज़ी से divide होते cells से भरा है। यही engine room है। Root जो भी cell कभी इस्तेमाल करेगा, वो यहीं बनता है।
फिर नए cells धकेल दिए जाते हैं zone of elongation में, जहाँ वो lambai में खिंचते हैं। Board देखिए — यही खिंचाव असल में root को soil में नीचे धकेलता है।
आख़िर में आता है zone of maturation, जहाँ cells अपने final forms में differentiate होते हैं और epidermis root hairs बाहर निकालती है।
इसी वजह से यही working zone है। Root hairs सिर्फ़ zone of maturation तक सीमित हैं और असल water और mineral absorption यही करते हैं। Lateral roots भी यहीं से originate होती हैं।
अब logic पकड़ लीजिए, क्योंकि logic ही आधे questions का जवाब है। पहले division, फिर elongation धकेलता है, फिर maturation काम करता है।
<whisper>मतलब absorption tip से थोड़ा पीछे है, बिल्कुल tip पर कभी नहीं। कोई option अगर root hairs को apex पर बिठा दे, तो वो पढ़ने से पहले ही ग़लत है।

board_events.text: Storage tap root: stores food and becomes swollen. Carrot, turnip.
Storage adventitious root: stores food. Sweet potato.
Prop or pillar roots: aerial roots hang down and support heavy branches. Banyan, Ficus benghalensis.
Stilt roots: from lower nodes of the stem, giving mechanical support. Maize, sugarcane, screwpine.
Pneumatophores: grow vertically up, negatively geotropic, for gas exchange. Mangroves: Rhizophora, Avicennia, Heritiera.
Store each as structure to job to one example. The bare term rarely earns the mark.

segments.text: A root modification is simply a root doing a job other than absorption and anchorage. Look at the board: four jobs, four shapes.
First, storage. A tap root can swell up and store food, and the standard examples are carrot and turnip. Same organ, thickened for the pantry.
Storage can also happen in an adventitious root, and the example you must have ready is sweet potato. Note it carefully: this is a root, not a stem.

Second, support from above. Prop roots, also called pillar roots, are aerial roots that hang down from branches to the ground and then support those heavy branches. The example is the banyan, Ficus benghalensis.
Third, support from below. Stilt roots arise from the lower nodes of the stem and brace the plant against toppling. The examples are maize, sugarcane, and screwpine.
Fourth, breathing. Pneumatophores, or respiratory roots, grow vertically upward, against gravity, because they are negatively geotropic, and they handle gas exchange in waterlogged mud.
That is the mangrove specialty, and the names are Rhizophora, Avicennia, and Heritiera. Waterlogged soil has no air in it, so the roots go up to fetch some.
<excited>And here is the storage rule for all of them. Keep each as a triplet: structure, then job, then one example. Stilt root, support, sugarcane. The bare term on its own rarely earns the mark.
Root modification का मतलब है root किसी और काम में लगा है, absorption और anchorage के अलावा। Board देखिए — चार jobs, चार shapes।
पहला, storage। Tap root फूलकर food store कर सकता है, और standard examples हैं carrot और turnip। Organ वही, बस pantry के लिए मोटा हो गया।
Storage adventitious root में भी हो सकता है, और यहाँ example तैयार रखिए — sweet potato। ध्यान से note कीजिए — ये root है, stem नहीं।

दूसरा, ऊपर से support। Prop roots, जिन्हें pillar roots भी कहते हैं, aerial roots हैं जो branches से लटककर ज़मीन तक आती हैं और फिर उन्हीं भारी branches को सँभालती हैं। Example है banyan, यानी Ficus benghalensis।
तीसरा, नीचे से support। Stilt roots stem के lower nodes से निकलती हैं और plant को गिरने से बचाती हैं। Examples हैं maize, sugarcane, और screwpine।
चौथा, साँस लेना। Pneumatophores, यानी respiratory roots, gravity के ख़िलाफ़ सीधे ऊपर बढ़ती हैं क्योंकि वो negatively geotropic हैं, और waterlogged mud में gas exchange सँभालती हैं।
ये mangroves की speciality है, और नाम हैं Rhizophora, Avicennia, और Heritiera। Waterlogged soil में hava होती ही नहीं, तो roots ऊपर जाकर ले आती हैं।
<excited>और सबके लिए एक storage rule। हर एक को triplet की तरह रखिए — structure, फिर job, फिर एक example। Stilt root, support, sugarcane। अकेला term अक्सर mark नहीं दिलाता।

board_events.text: Underground stems: rhizome, tuber, corm, bulb.
Their jobs: storage, perennation, and vegetative propagation.
Examples: ginger (rhizome), potato (tuber), turmeric, zaminkand, Colocasia.
They keep nodes, scale-leaves and buds. That is why they stay stems.
Runner or stolon: a slender lateral branch from the base of the main axis; grows aerially, then arches down to root at the tip. Mint, jasmine.
Offset: a short, thick lateral branch with one internode, bearing a rosette of leaves and a tuft of roots. Aquatic spread: Pistia, Eichhornia.

segments.text: Stems get modified too, and the first family of modifications is the one that causes the most damage in exams: the stems that go underground.
Look at the board. The underground stems are the rhizome, the tuber, the corm, and the bulb. Four names, one address.
Their jobs come as a set of three. Storage, because food keeps well below ground. Perennation, which means surviving an unfavourable season underground and coming back. And vegetative propagation.
The examples you must have instantly: ginger is a rhizome, potato is a tuber, and turmeric, zaminkand and Colocasia complete the list.
Now the reason they stay stems, however deep they sit. They keep their nodes, their scale-leaves, and their buds. The features travelled underground with them.

The second family is subaerial: stems that run along the surface. A runner, also called a stolon, is a slender lateral branch that arises from the base of the main axis, grows aerially, and then arches down to root at its tip.
That rooting tip is the point of the whole exercise. It is vegetative spread, and the examples are mint and jasmine. The plant walks sideways without seeds.

An offset is the aquatic version: a short, thick lateral branch with just one internode, bearing a rosette of leaves and a tuft of roots. It spreads floating plants, and the examples are Pistia and Eichhornia.
Stems भी modify होते हैं, और modifications का पहला family वही है जो exams में सबसे ज़्यादा नुक़सान करता है — वो stems जो ज़मीन के नीचे चले जाते हैं।
Board देखिए। Underground stems हैं rhizome, tuber, corm, और bulb। चार नाम, एक पता।
इनके jobs तीन का set हैं। Storage, क्योंकि ज़मीन के नीचे food अच्छा रहता है। Perennation, यानी ख़राब मौसम नीचे काटकर वापस आ जाना। और vegetative propagation।
Examples तुरंत तैयार होने चाहिए — ginger एक rhizome है, potato एक tuber, और turmeric, zaminkand तथा Colocasia list पूरी करते हैं।
अब वजह कि ये कितने भी गहरे बैठें, stems ही रहते हैं। इनके nodes, scale-leaves, और buds इनके साथ ही रहते हैं। Features इनके साथ नीचे चले गए।

दूसरा family है subaerial — वो stems जो surface पर दौड़ते हैं। Runner, जिसे stolon भी कहते हैं, एक slender lateral branch है जो main axis के base से निकलती है, aerially बढ़ती है, और फिर झुककर अपने tip से root कर लेती है।
वही rooting tip पूरी कहानी का point है। ये vegetative spread है, और examples हैं mint और jasmine। Plant बिना seeds के बग़ल में चल पड़ता है।

Offset इसका aquatic version है — एक छोटी, मोटी lateral branch जिसमें सिर्फ़ एक internode होता है, ऊपर leaves का rosette और नीचे roots का tuft। ये floating plants को फैलाता है, examples हैं Pistia और Eichhornia।

board_events.text: Stem tendril: spirally coiled, thread-like, and sensitive.
Job: climbing. It arises from an axillary bud.
Examples: cucumber, pumpkin, watermelon, grapevine.
Thorn: a hard, pointed, woody structure. Job: protection from grazing and browsing animals.
Examples: Citrus, Bougainvillea.
Both arise from axillary buds, so both are modified SHOOTS, not leaves.

segments.text: The last family of stem modifications stays up in the air, and it holds two structures that look nothing alike but share one origin.
The first is the stem tendril. It is spirally coiled, thread-like, and sensitive, which means it responds to touch by winding around whatever it meets.
Its job is climbing. A weak-stemmed plant cannot hold itself up, so it borrows support, and the tendril is the grappling hook. Crucially, it arises from an axillary bud.
The examples are the cucurbits and the vine: cucumber, pumpkin, watermelon, and grapevine. If a climber has coiling threads, this is the family to think of first.
The second is the thorn: a hard, pointed, woody structure whose job is protection from grazing and browsing animals. The plant makes itself painful to eat.
The examples here are Citrus and Bougainvillea, and please store them as a pair, because these two turn up in matching questions almost every year.
Now look at the board and take the point that ties them together. Both the tendril and the thorn arise from axillary buds.
<curious>And what arises from an axillary bud? A shoot. So both are modified shoots, not leaves, however soft or however sharp they look. That shared origin is the exam-critical line here.
Stem modifications का आख़िरी family हवा में ही रहता है, और इसमें दो structures हैं जो दिखने में बिल्कुल अलग हैं पर origin एक ही है।
पहला है stem tendril। ये spirally coiled है, thread-like है, और sensitive है — यानी छूने पर react करता है और जो मिले उसी के चारों ओर लिपट जाता है।
इसका job है climbing। Weak-stemmed plant ख़ुद को सँभाल नहीं सकता, तो वो support उधार लेता है, और tendril उसका grappling hook है। सबसे ज़रूरी — ये axillary bud से निकलता है।
Examples हैं cucurbits और vine — cucumber, pumpkin, watermelon, और grapevine। किसी climber पर लिपटते धागे दिखें तो सबसे पहले यही family सोचिए।
दूसरा है thorn — एक hard, pointed, woody structure जिसका job है grazing और browsing animals से protection। Plant ख़ुद को खाने में दर्दनाक बना लेता है।
यहाँ examples हैं Citrus और Bougainvillea, और इन्हें जोड़े में ही store कीजिए, क्योंकि ये दोनों matching questions में लगभग हर साल आते हैं।
अब board देखिए और वो point पकड़िए जो दोनों को जोड़ता है। Tendril और thorn, दोनों axillary buds से निकलते हैं।
<curious>और axillary bud से निकलता क्या है? Shoot। तो दोनों modified shoots हैं, leaves नहीं — चाहे कितने भी नरम या कितने भी नुकीले दिखें। यही shared origin यहाँ की exam-critical line है।

board_events.text: Leaf base: attaches the leaf to the stem; may bear two lateral stipules.
Petiole: the stalk that holds the blade out into the light.
Lamina or leaf blade: the flat green photosynthetic part.
Within the lamina: midrib, veins, and veinlets. The leaf's plumbing and skeleton at once.
Upper surface = adaxial. Lower surface = abaxial.
The axillary bud sits in the axil, where leaf base meets stem: your single best clue.

segments.text: Labelling a dicot leaf is guaranteed board marks, and the way to never lose them is to trace the leaf in one direction: from the stem outward.
It starts at the leaf base, the part that attaches the leaf to the stem. And the leaf base may carry two lateral stipules, small appendages on either side.
From the base rises the petiole, the stalk. Its job is simple and mechanical: hold the blade out into the light, away from the shade of the stem.
The petiole then expands into the lamina, also called the leaf blade. This is the flat green photosynthetic part, the piece doing the actual work.
Run a finger down the middle of the lamina and you meet the midrib, and from it the veins and finer veinlets spread out. Look at the board: these are the leaf's plumbing and its skeleton at once.
Two surface terms finish the picture. The upper surface is adaxial and the lower surface is abaxial. Adaxial faces the axis, and that is the memory hook.
Now the piece that pays off later. Sitting in the angle between the leaf base and the stem is the axillary bud.
<whisper>That bud is your single best clue in the next structure we take up. Where the bud sits decides whether you are looking at one leaf or at a whole branch.
Dicot leaf को label करना board के pakke marks हैं, और इन्हें न गँवाने का तरीक़ा है — leaf को एक ही direction में trace कीजिए, stem से बाहर की ओर।
शुरुआत होती है leaf base से, यानी वो हिस्सा जो leaf को stem से जोड़ता है। और leaf base पर दो lateral stipules हो सकते हैं, दोनों तरफ़ छोटे appendages।
Base से उठता है petiole, यानी डंठल। इसका काम simple और mechanical है — blade को light में बाहर पकड़े रखना, stem की छाँव से दूर।
फिर petiole फैलकर बनता है lamina, जिसे leaf blade भी कहते हैं। यही flat green photosynthetic हिस्सा है, असल काम यही करता है।
Lamina के बीचोंबीच उँगली फेरिए तो midrib मिलेगा, और उसी से veins तथा बारीक veinlets फैलते हैं। Board देखिए — ये एक साथ leaf की plumbing भी हैं और skeleton भी।
दो surface terms तस्वीर पूरी कर देते हैं। ऊपर वाली surface adaxial, नीचे वाली abaxial। Adaxial axis की तरफ़ होती है — यही memory hook है।
अब वो हिस्सा जो आगे काम आएगा। Leaf base और stem के बीच के angle में बैठता है axillary bud।
<whisper>अगले structure में वही bud आपका सबसे बड़ा clue है। Bud कहाँ बैठा है, यही तय करता है कि आप एक leaf देख रहे हैं या पूरी branch।

board_events.text: Venation: the arrangement of veins in the lamina.
Reticulate = net-like = characteristic of DICOTS. Parallel = characteristic of MONOCOTS.
Simple leaf: a single, undivided lamina.
Its margin may be incised: to half (-fid), past half (-partite), or nearly to the midrib (-sect). Forms like pinnatifid, palmatifid.
However deep the incision, it never cuts the lamina into separate parts. Still simple.
Compound leaf: lamina genuinely broken into leaflets. Pinnately compound (neem) or palmately compound (silk cotton).

segments.text: Two features of the lamina now, and both are exam favourites for opposite reasons: one because it is easy, one because it is subtle.
The easy one first. Venation is the arrangement of veins in the lamina, and there are two patterns.
Reticulate venation is net-like, and it is characteristic of dicots. Parallel venation is characteristic of monocots. Look at the board and anchor it once: net equals dicot, parallel equals mono.
Anchor it now, because half the venation questions are worded to tempt you into the exact reversal, and a reversal costs a full mark on a question you actually knew.
Now the subtle one. A simple leaf has a single, undivided lamina. That word undivided is doing all the work here.

Because a simple leaf's margin may be incised, and quite deeply. Incised up to half is a fid form, more than half is partite, and nearly to the midrib or base is sect, giving forms such as pinnatifid and palmatifid.
But look carefully at the board. However deep those incisions run, they never cut the lamina into separate parts. The blade is still one piece, so the leaf is still simple.

A compound leaf is the real thing: the lamina is genuinely broken into distinct leaflets. It is pinnately compound when leaflets sit along a central rachis, as in neem, and palmately compound when they all attach at the petiole tip, as in silk cotton.
अब lamina के दो features, और दोनों exam के favourite हैं — उल्टी वजहों से। एक इसलिए कि वो आसान है, दूसरा इसलिए कि वो subtle है।
पहले आसान वाला। Venation यानी lamina में veins की arrangement, और patterns दो हैं।

Reticulate venation net-like होती है, और ये dicots की characteristic है। Parallel venation monocots की characteristic है। Board देखिए और एक बार में anchor कर लीजिए — net यानी dicot, parallel यानी mono।
अभी anchor कीजिए, क्योंकि venation के आधे questions आपको ठीक उल्टा करने के लिए ही लिखे जाते हैं, और वो उल्टा एक पूरा mark ले जाता है — उस question पर जो आपको आता था।
अब subtle वाला। Simple leaf में lamina single और undivided होती है। पूरा काम यहाँ वही शब्द कर रहा है — undivided।

क्योंकि simple leaf का margin incised हो सकता है, और काफ़ी गहरा भी। आधे तक incised हो तो fid form, आधे से ज़्यादा हो तो partite, और लगभग midrib या base तक हो तो sect — जिससे pinnatifid और palmatifid जैसे forms बनते हैं।
पर board को ध्यान से देखिए। ये incisions चाहे कितने भी गहरे जाएँ, lamina को अलग-अलग हिस्सों में कभी नहीं काटते। Blade अब भी एक ही टुकड़ा है, तो leaf अब भी simple है।

Compound leaf असली बँटवारा है — यहाँ lamina सचमुच अलग leaflets में टूट जाती है। Leaflets अगर central rachis पर हों तो pinnately compound, जैसे neem; और सब petiole के tip पर जुड़े हों तो palmately compound, जैसे silk cotton।

board_events.text: The problem: a pinnately compound leaf looks exactly like a small branch bearing leaflets.
The clean test: a bud sits in the axil of a WHOLE leaf, never in the axils of individual leaflets.
Step one: locate the leaflets.
Step two: hunt for axillary buds between them.
Step three: no buds between them, one bud at the base of the whole structure, means a single compound leaf.
Buds tucked between the 'leaflets' means a branch with simple leaves.

segments.text: Students lose easy marks confusing a pinnately compound leaf with a small branch, and the reason is honest: on paper the two look identical.
Both show an axis. Both show green flaps arranged along that axis. Staring harder at the flaps will not help you, because the flaps are not where the information is.
Here is the clean test, and it comes straight from what we established about the leaf. A bud sits in the axil of a whole leaf, but never in the axils of the individual leaflets of a compound leaf.
So run it as three steps. Step one: locate the leaflets. Just find the flaps and stop judging them.
Step two: hunt for axillary buds between them. Look at the joints along the axis, one by one, and ask whether a bud is tucked in.
Step three: if there are no buds between them, and one bud at the base of the whole structure, then the whole structure is a single compound leaf and that axis is a rachis.
Look at the right-hand side of the board for the other verdict. If you see buds tucked between the leaflets, you are not looking at leaflets at all.
<chuckle>You are looking at a branch with simple leaves, each with its own bud, exactly as leaves are supposed to have. The structure was never one leaf. The buds told you, not the shape.
Students आसान marks इसीलिए गँवाते हैं क्योंकि pinnately compound leaf और छोटी branch में confuse हो जाते हैं, और वजह जायज़ है — काग़ज़ पर दोनों एक जैसे दिखते हैं।
दोनों में एक axis है। दोनों में उस axis पर green flaps लगे हैं। Flaps को और घूरने से फ़ायदा नहीं, क्योंकि information flaps में है ही नहीं।
यही है clean test, और ये सीधे उसी बात से आता है जो हमने leaf के बारे में तय की थी। Bud पूरी leaf के axil में बैठता है, पर compound leaf के अलग-अलग leaflets के axils में कभी नहीं।
तो इसे तीन steps में चलाइए। Step one — leaflets locate कीजिए। बस flaps ढूँढिए, उन पर judgement मत दीजिए।
Step two — उनके बीच axillary buds खोजिए। Axis के हर joint को एक-एक करके देखिए और पूछिए कि वहाँ कोई bud छिपा है क्या।
Step three — अगर उनके बीच कोई bud नहीं है, और पूरे structure के base पर एक bud है, तो पूरा structure एक ही compound leaf है और वो axis एक rachis है।
दूसरा verdict के लिए board का दायाँ हिस्सा देखिए। अगर leaflets के बीच buds दिख रहे हैं, तो आप leaflets देख ही नहीं रहे।
<chuckle>आप एक branch देख रहे हैं जिस पर simple leaves लगी हैं, हर एक के अपने bud के साथ — ठीक वैसे जैसे leaves के होने चाहिए। ये structure कभी एक leaf थी ही नहीं। Shape ने नहीं, buds ने बताया।

board_events.text: Phyllotaxy: the arrangement of leaves on the stem.
Alternate: one leaf per node. Mango, mustard, sunflower, china rose.
Opposite: two leaves per node. Calotropis, guava.
Whorled: more than two leaves per node. Nerium.
Leaf modifications: fleshy storage leaves (onion, garlic); insectivorous traps (pitcher plant, Venus flytrap); leaf tendrils.
Bryophyllum and Begonia bear adventitious buds on the leaf: a leaf that propagates.

segments.text: Two loose ends on the leaf, and both are pure marks if you keep the examples attached.
The first is phyllotaxy: the arrangement of leaves on the stem. Look at the board, and notice that the whole classification turns on one number, how many leaves sit at a node.
One leaf per node is alternate phyllotaxy, and the examples are mango, mustard, sunflower, and china rose.
Two leaves per node is opposite phyllotaxy, and the examples are Calotropis and guava.
More than two per node is whorled phyllotaxy, and the standard example is Nerium. So: count the leaves at one node and the answer names itself.
The second loose end is leaf modification, the leaf doing something other than photosynthesis. Fleshy storage leaves hold food, as in onion and garlic.
Insectivorous traps catch prey, as in the pitcher plant and the Venus flytrap. And leaf tendrils climb, which is why you must always ask whether a tendril came from a leaf or from a shoot.
<excited>And the best one: leaves bearing adventitious buds for vegetative propagation, in Bryophyllum and Begonia. New plantlets from a leaf margin. Propagation is not only a stem or root affair.
अब leaf के दो loose ends, और दोनों pakke marks हैं — बशर्ते examples साथ चिपके रहें।
पहला है phyllotaxy — यानी stem पर leaves की arrangement। Board देखिए, और ध्यान दीजिए कि पूरी classification एक ही number पर टिकी है — एक node पर कितनी leaves हैं।
एक node पर एक leaf यानी alternate phyllotaxy, और examples हैं mango, mustard, sunflower, और china rose।
एक node पर दो leaves यानी opposite phyllotaxy, और examples हैं Calotropis और guava।
एक node पर दो से ज़्यादा यानी whorled phyllotaxy, और standard example है Nerium। तो बस एक node पर leaves गिनिए, जवाब ख़ुद अपना नाम बता देगा।
दूसरा loose end है leaf modification — यानी leaf photosynthesis छोड़कर कुछ और कर रही है। Fleshy storage leaves food रखती हैं, जैसे onion और garlic में।
Insectivorous traps शिकार पकड़ती हैं, जैसे pitcher plant और Venus flytrap। और leaf tendrils चढ़ती हैं — इसीलिए हमेशा पूछिए कि tendril leaf से आया है या shoot से।

<excited>और सबसे मज़ेदार — वो leaves जिन पर vegetative propagation के लिए adventitious buds होते हैं, Bryophyllum और Begonia में। Leaf के margin से नए plantlets। Propagation सिर्फ़ stem या root का काम नहीं है।

board_events.text: Check one, nodes and internodes: scrape the surface and look for repeating points bearing scale-leaves or buds.
A horizontal ginger 'hand' shows clear nodes carrying scaly leaves with buds in their axils. That alone marks it a stem: a rhizome.
Check two, buds: a potato's eyes are axillary buds at nodes. Eyes settle it as a stem: a tuber.
Check three, hairs and direction: a true storage root is smooth, lacks nodes and buds, and tapers like a continuation of the main axis.
Carrot and sweet potato pass check three: they are roots.
Rule of thumb: nodes, scale-leaves or buds mean STEM, no matter how deep it sits.

segments.text: Let us turn everything so far into one routine you can run in the exam hall in about ten seconds. Hand-test any swollen underground part with three checks, in this order.
Check one is nodes and internodes. Mentally scrape the surface and look for repeating points from which scale-leaves or buds arise.
Take a horizontal ginger hand. It shows clear nodes carrying scaly leaves, with buds in their axils. That alone marks it a stem, and its name is a rhizome. You can stop there.
Check two is buds, and it is your fallback when the nodes are not obvious. A potato's eyes are axillary buds sitting at nodes.
Eyes settle it. The potato is a stem, and its name is a tuber. Notice that both checks so far are looking for the same thing: shoot features that survived the journey underground.

Check three is hairs and direction, and this is the one that confirms a root. A true storage root, like carrot or sweet potato, is smooth, lacks nodes and buds, and tapers like a continuation of the main axis.
So carrot and sweet potato fail checks one and two and pass check three. They are roots, and they are storage roots.
And the rule of thumb that carries all three: if it carries nodes, scale-leaves, or buds, it is a stem, no matter how deep it sits.
अब तक की हर बात को एक routine में बदल देते हैं, जिसे आप exam hall में क़रीब दस second में चला सकें। किसी भी swollen underground part को तीन checks से हाथ में लेकर परखिए, इसी order में।
Check one — nodes और internodes। दिमाग़ में surface को खुरचिए और ऐसे repeating points ढूँढिए जहाँ से scale-leaves या buds निकल रहे हों।
एक horizontal ginger का hand लीजिए। उसमें साफ़ nodes हैं, उन पर scaly leaves, और उनके axils में buds। बस इतने से ही वो stem साबित हो गया, और उसका नाम है rhizome। यहीं रुक जाइए।
Check two — buds, और ये तब काम आता है जब nodes साफ़ न दिखें। Potato की eyes असल में nodes पर बैठे axillary buds हैं।
Eyes faisla कर देती हैं। Potato एक stem है, और उसका नाम है tuber। ध्यान दीजिए, अब तक दोनों checks एक ही चीज़ ढूँढ रहे हैं — shoot के वो features जो ज़मीन के नीचे भी बचे रहे।

Check three — hairs और direction, और यही root को confirm करता है। सच्चा storage root, जैसे carrot या sweet potato, smooth होता है, उसमें nodes और buds नहीं होते, और वो main axis के continuation की तरह taper होता है।
तो carrot और sweet potato check one और two में fail होते हैं और check three पास कर लेते हैं। ये roots हैं, और storage roots हैं।
और वो rule of thumb जो तीनों checks को उठा लेता है — जिसमें nodes, scale-leaves या buds हों, वो stem है, चाहे वो कितना भी गहरा बैठा हो।

board_events.text: Step two, apply it to the potato: though it grows underground, it has small depressions called eyes.
Each eye is a node bearing an axillary bud, a feature only a stem can have.
Now the sweet potato: a swollen organ with no nodes and no buds. It is an adventitious root modified for storage.
Answer: potato has buds at nodes, so stem (tuber); sweet potato has none, so root (storage adventitious root).

segments.text: First worked example, and it is board level: give one defining difference between a root and a stem, and use it to explain why a potato is a stem while a sweet potato is a root.
Notice the structure of the question. It asks for a feature and then for an application. So step one is to state the defining feature cleanly, before touching either plant.
Here it is. A stem bears nodes, internodes and buds, whereas a root has none of these. Say it in that shape, as a contrast, because the contrast is what earns the first mark.
Now apply it, and look at the board while we do. Two organs, one basket, and one feature that separates them.
Take the potato. Though it grows underground, it has small depressions on its surface, the things we call eyes.
And each eye is a node bearing an axillary bud, which is a feature only a stem can have. That is the whole argument. Not its depth, not its shape, not its starch. Its buds.
Now the sweet potato. It is a swollen organ with no nodes and no buds at all. So it fails the stem test on every count, and it is an adventitious root modified for storage.

Write the answer as the examiner wants it. Presence of nodes, internodes and buds is the defining feature of a stem. The potato has buds at nodes, so it is a stem, a tuber. The sweet potato has none, so it is a root, a storage adventitious root.
पहला worked example, और ये board level है — root और stem में एक defining difference बताइए, और उसी से समझाइए कि potato stem क्यों है और sweet potato root।
Question की बनावट देखिए। पहले एक feature माँगा है, फिर उसका application। तो step one — feature को साफ़-साफ़ बताइए, किसी भी plant को छूने से पहले।
ये रहा। Stem में nodes, internodes और buds होते हैं, जबकि root में इनमें से कुछ नहीं होता। इसी shape में, contrast की तरह कहिए, क्योंकि पहला mark यही contrast दिलाता है।
अब इसे apply कीजिए, और साथ में board देखिए। दो organs, एक basket, और एक feature जो इन्हें अलग करता है।
Potato लीजिए। ज़मीन के नीचे उगने के बावजूद, उसकी surface पर छोटे-छोटे गड्ढे होते हैं — जिन्हें हम eyes कहते हैं।
और हर eye एक node है जिस पर axillary bud है — ऐसा feature जो सिर्फ़ stem के पास हो सकता है। पूरी दलील बस यही है। न उसकी depth, न shape, न starch। उसके buds।
अब sweet potato। ये एक swollen organ है जिसमें न nodes हैं न buds। तो वो stem test में हर point पर fail है, और वो storage के लिए modified एक adventitious root है।

जवाब वैसे ही लिखिए जैसे examiner चाहता है। Nodes, internodes और buds की presence stem का defining feature है। Potato में nodes पर buds हैं, तो वो stem है — tuber। Sweet potato में कुछ नहीं, तो वो root है — storage adventitious root।

sections.title: Worked example two: assertion and reason on fibrous anchorage

board_events.text: Entrance level, assertion-reason: does a fibrous system anchor better in shallow, loose topsoil?
Assertion: a fibrous root system anchors a plant more securely than a tap root system in shallow, loose topsoil.
Reason: in a fibrous system, numerous roots arise from the base of the stem and spread through the surface soil.
Test the reason first: it is factually correct, a dense mat of roots from the stem base occupying the surface layer.

board_events.text: Now the real question: does that mat explain better anchorage in loose topsoil?
Yes. Many roots spread laterally grip a wide patch of shallow soil, like the many guy-ropes of a tent against a single peg.
Answer: (a) both true, and the reason is the correct explanation of the assertion.

segments.text: Second example, and it is an assertion-reason item, which is a format that punishes speed. Read the board.
The assertion says a fibrous root system anchors a plant to the soil more securely than a tap root system in shallow, loose topsoil.
The reason says that in a fibrous system, numerous roots arise from the base of the stem and spread through the surface soil.

Now the technique, and it is always the same. Test the reason first, because a reason is usually a plain fact and facts are quicker to settle. Here it is factually correct: a fibrous system really is a dense mat of roots originating from the stem base, occupying the surface layer.
So the reason is true, and now comes the part students rush. A true reason is not automatically the explanation. Look at the board and ask the real question.
Does that mat explain better anchorage specifically in loose topsoil? That is the claim you must judge, not whether fibrous roots exist.

And the answer is yes. Many roots spread laterally grip a wide patch of shallow soil, exactly like the many guy-ropes of a tent versus a single peg. The tap root drives deep, but in loose topsoil there is nothing firm down there to hold.
So the assertion is true, the reason is true, and the reason is its correct cause. The answer is option (a).
दूसरा example, और ये assertion-reason है — ऐसा format जो जल्दबाज़ी को सज़ा देता है। Board पढ़िए।
Assertion कहता है कि shallow, loose topsoil में fibrous root system, tap root system के मुक़ाबले plant को ज़्यादा मज़बूती से anchor करता है।
Reason कहता है कि fibrous system में बहुत सारी roots stem के base से निकलती हैं और surface soil में फैल जाती हैं।

अब technique, और ये हमेशा वही रहती है। पहले reason को test कीजिए, क्योंकि reason आम तौर पर एक सीधा fact होता है और facts जल्दी settle होते हैं। यहाँ ये factually सही है — fibrous system वाक़ई stem base से निकली roots की dense mat है जो surface layer में फैली रहती है।
तो reason true है, और अब वो हिस्सा आता है जहाँ students जल्दी कर जाते हैं। True reason अपने आप explanation नहीं बन जाता। Board देखिए और असली सवाल पूछिए।
क्या वो mat ख़ास तौर पर loose topsoil में बेहतर anchorage को explain करती है? यही claim आपको जाँचना है, ये नहीं कि fibrous roots होती हैं या नहीं।

और जवाब है — हाँ। बहुत सारी roots बग़ल में फैलकर shallow soil का एक चौड़ा टुकड़ा पकड़ती हैं, बिल्कुल tent की कई guy-ropes बनाम एक अकेले peg की तरह। Tap root गहरा जाता है, पर loose topsoil में नीचे पकड़ने लायक़ कुछ है ही नहीं।
तो assertion true, reason true, और reason ही उसकी सही वजह है। जवाब है option (a)।

board_events.text: W: vertical, upward roots from waterlogged anaerobic mud means pneumatophores, negatively geotropic respiratory roots.
X: thick roots descending from the branches of a fig to support them means prop roots.
Y: a dense tuft of fine roots from the stem base of a cereal, a monocot, means a fibrous root system.
Z: a single swollen storage organ that is a true root means a storage tap root.

segments.text: Third example, entrance level, and it is the format that decides matching questions: four observations, four verdicts.

A botany student examines four plants along a tidal mangrove creek and a riverbank. Plant W has roots growing vertically upward out of the waterlogged mud. Plant X, a large fig tree, has thick roots hanging from its branches down to the ground.
Plant Y, a cereal, has a dense tuft of fine roots from the stem base. Plant Z has a swollen orange storage root. Match each to the correct root type.
Do not read all four and then guess. Look at the board and work feature by feature, one plant at a time, and the question falls apart on its own.

Plant W. Vertical, upward roots out of waterlogged, anaerobic mud. Upward growth against gravity means negatively geotropic, and mud with no air means the job is gas exchange. Those are pneumatophores, the respiratory roots.

Plant X. Thick roots descending from the branches of a fig to support them. Descending from branches is the giveaway: these are prop roots. If they had come from the lower stem nodes they would have been stilt roots instead.
Plant Y. A dense tuft of fine roots from the stem base of a cereal, and a cereal is a monocot. Roots from the stem base, not the radicle. That is a fibrous root system.
Plant Z. A single swollen storage organ that is a true root, so a storage tap root. Final answer: W pneumatophores, X prop roots, Y fibrous roots, Z storage tap root.
तीसरा example, entrance level, और यही वो format है जो matching questions तय करता है — चार observations, चार verdicts।

एक botany student एक tidal mangrove creek और riverbank पर चार plants देखता है। Plant W में roots waterlogged mud से सीधे ऊपर की ओर बढ़ रही हैं। Plant X, एक बड़ा fig tree, जिसकी branches से मोटी roots लटककर ज़मीन तक आ रही हैं।
Plant Y, एक cereal, जिसमें stem base से बारीक roots का घना tuft है। Plant Z में एक swollen orange storage root है। हर एक को सही root type से match कीजिए।
चारों पढ़कर अंदाज़ा मत लगाइए। Board देखिए और feature by feature चलिए, एक बार में एक plant — question ख़ुद ही बिखर जाएगा।

Plant W। Waterlogged, anaerobic mud से सीधी ऊपर जाती roots। Gravity के ख़िलाफ़ ऊपर बढ़ना यानी negatively geotropic, और बिना hava वाली mud यानी काम है gas exchange। ये pneumatophores हैं, यानी respiratory roots।
Plant X। Fig की branches से उतरकर उन्हीं को सँभालती मोटी roots। Branches से उतरना ही giveaway है — ये prop roots हैं। अगर यही lower stem nodes से आतीं, तो stilt roots होतीं।
Plant Y। Cereal के stem base से बारीक roots का घना tuft, और cereal एक monocot है। Roots stem base से हैं, radicle से नहीं। यही fibrous root system है।
Plant Z। एक अकेला swollen storage organ जो सचमुच root है, तो storage tap root। Final answer — W pneumatophores, X prop roots, Y fibrous roots, Z storage tap root।

board_events.text: Statement one: stem tendrils develop from axillary buds in cucurbits; thorns in Citrus and Bougainvillea are also modified shoots from axillary buds. TRUE.
Statement two: Bryophyllum leaves carry adventitious buds at the margins that grow into new plantlets. TRUE.
Trap one: the reflex that tendrils and thorns are different things, so the statement must be false.
Trap two: assuming propagation is only ever by stem or root. Both statements are true and independent.

segments.text: Fourth example, and it is the high-difficulty format: two statements, evaluate both, and identify the trap. This is where careless students lose a question they knew.
Statement one says stem tendrils and thorns can both arise from axillary buds.
Statement two says that in Bryophyllum, new plantlets arise from buds borne on the leaf margin, which is an example of a leaf functioning as an organ of vegetative propagation.
Rule for this format: evaluate each statement completely on its own, before you look at the pair. Look at the board, where we have done exactly that.

Statement one. Stem tendrils develop from axillary buds, as in the cucurbits. And thorns, in plants such as Citrus and Bougainvillea, are also modified shoots arising from axillary buds. So statement one is true.
Statement two. Bryophyllum leaves carry adventitious buds at the margins that grow into new plantlets. That is a genuine case of the leaf as a propagation organ, so statement two is true as well.

Now the traps, and there are two. The first is the reflex: tendrils and thorns are different things, they look nothing alike, so surely the statement must be false. But the statement is about origin, not appearance, and their origin is shared.

The second trap is assuming propagation is only ever by stem or root. Bryophyllum simply does not care about your assumption. So: both statements are true, and neither explains the other. They are independent facts. The distractor is treating a thorn as non-shoot in origin.
चौथा example, और ये high-difficulty format है — दो statements, दोनों evaluate कीजिए, और trap पहचानिए। यहीं careless students वो question गँवाते हैं जो उन्हें आता था।
Statement one कहता है कि stem tendrils और thorns, दोनों axillary buds से निकल सकते हैं।
Statement two कहता है कि Bryophyllum में नए plantlets leaf के margin पर लगे buds से निकलते हैं, जो leaf के vegetative propagation का organ होने का example है।
इस format का rule — हर statement को अलग-अलग, पूरा evaluate कीजिए, जोड़ी देखने से पहले। Board देखिए, वहाँ हमने ठीक यही किया है।

Statement one। Stem tendrils axillary buds से develop होते हैं, जैसे cucurbits में। और thorns — Citrus तथा Bougainvillea जैसे plants में — भी axillary buds से निकले modified shoots हैं। तो statement one true है।
Statement two। Bryophyllum की leaves के margins पर adventitious buds होते हैं जो नए plantlets बन जाते हैं। ये leaf के propagation organ होने का सच्चा case है, तो statement two भी true है।

अब traps, और वो दो हैं। पहला है reflex — tendrils और thorns तो अलग चीज़ें हैं, दिखने में ज़रा भी नहीं मिलतीं, तो statement ग़लत ही होगा। पर statement origin की बात कर रहा है, appearance की नहीं, और origin इनका साझा है।

दूसरा trap है ये मान लेना कि propagation सिर्फ़ stem या root से ही होता है। Bryophyllum को आपकी इस assumption से कोई मतलब नहीं। तो — दोनों statements true हैं, और कोई किसी को explain नहीं करता। ये independent facts हैं। Distractor है thorn को non-shoot origin मान लेना।

sections.subtopic: The Root, the Stem, and the Leaf
sections.title: Pitfalls and pro-tips for the root, the stem and the leaf

board_events.text: Four pitfalls that cost marks here, and two habits that save them
Pitfall one: 'underground means root'. Ginger, turmeric, potato, zaminkand and Colocasia are underground stems.
Always check for nodes and buds, never depth in the soil.
Pitfall two, the potato and sweet potato swap: potato = stem tuber (eyes, buds at nodes); sweet potato = storage root (no buds).
Pitfall three, venation reversal. Anchor it once: net = dicot, parallel = monocot.
Pitfall four, calling a compound leaf a branch. The bud test settles it: a bud sits in the axil of a whole leaf, never between leaflets.
Pro-tip: store every modification as a triplet, structure to job to one example. 'Stilt root, support, sugarcane' earns the mark; 'stilt root' alone usually does not.
Pro-tip: transverse section, vascular bundles or casparian strips means you have crossed into anatomy. The answer lives in a different chapter.

segments.text: Let us close the subtopic with the four pitfalls that actually cost marks here, and the two habits that save them.
Pitfall one, and it is the biggest in the whole topic: underground means root. It does not. Ginger, turmeric, potato, zaminkand and Colocasia are all underground stems.
So the correction is a habit, not a fact. Always check for nodes and buds, never for depth in the soil. Depth has never been a defining feature of anything.

Pitfall two is the potato and sweet potato swap, and it is so common it has its own reputation. Potato is a stem tuber, because it has eyes, which are buds at nodes. Sweet potato is a storage root, with no buds at all.
Pitfall three is venation reversal. Anchor it once and never revisit it: net equals dicot, parallel equals monocot. Half the venation questions are deliberately worded to tempt the reversal.
Pitfall four is calling a compound leaf a branch. The bud test settles it every time: a bud sits in the axil of a whole leaf, never between leaflets. Look for buds, not for shape.

Now the first pro-tip, and it changes how you revise. For every root or stem modification, store it as a triplet: structure, then job, then one example. Entrance papers almost always ask the example or the function, rarely the bare term. Stilt root, support, sugarcane earns the mark. Stilt root alone usually does not.

And the second pro-tip is a tripwire. The instant a question mentions a transverse section, or vascular bundles, or casparian strips, flag it. You have crossed from morphology into anatomy, and the answer lives in a different chapter entirely.
अब subtopic बंद करते हैं उन चार pitfalls के साथ जो यहाँ सचमुच marks ले जाते हैं, और उन दो habits के साथ जो marks बचाती हैं।
Pitfall one, और यही पूरे topic का सबसे बड़ा है — underground यानी root। नहीं। Ginger, turmeric, potato, zaminkand और Colocasia — सब underground stems हैं।
तो correction एक habit है, कोई fact नहीं। हमेशा nodes और buds check कीजिए, कभी soil की depth नहीं। Depth कभी किसी चीज़ का defining feature था ही नहीं।

Pitfall two है potato और sweet potato की अदला-बदली, और ये इतना आम है कि इसकी अपनी reputation है। Potato एक stem tuber है, क्योंकि उसमें eyes हैं — यानी nodes पर buds। Sweet potato एक storage root है, जिसमें एक भी bud नहीं।
Pitfall three है venation reversal। एक बार anchor कीजिए और दोबारा मत खोलिए — net यानी dicot, parallel यानी monocot। Venation के आधे questions जानबूझकर उल्टा कराने के लिए लिखे जाते हैं।
Pitfall four है compound leaf को branch कह देना। Bud test हर बार faisla कर देता है — bud पूरी leaf के axil में बैठता है, leaflets के बीच कभी नहीं। Buds ढूँढिए, shape नहीं।

अब पहला pro-tip, और ये आपकी revision बदल देगा। हर root या stem modification को triplet की तरह store कीजिए — structure, फिर job, फिर एक example। Entrance papers लगभग हमेशा example या function पूछते हैं, अकेला term शायद ही। Stilt root, support, sugarcane — mark मिलेगा। अकेला stilt root — आम तौर पर नहीं।

और दूसरा pro-tip एक tripwire है। जिस पल question में transverse section, या vascular bundles, या casparian strips आए — flag कर दीजिए। आप morphology से anatomy में चले गए हैं, और जवाब पूरी तरह किसी दूसरे chapter में है।

board_events.text: When a flowering plant is ready to reproduce, its shoot tip stops making leaves and starts making a flower instead.
A flower is a shoot whose growing tip has been reprogrammed to produce floral parts at its nodes rather than ordinary leaves.
The internodes do not elongate, so all the parts sit crowded on a compressed axis.
That is why a flower looks like a tight rosette rather than a long stalk.
The swollen tip of that compressed axis is the thalamus, and the whorls are borne on it.
So every floral part you will name is a leaf-position occupied by something else.

segments.text: In the last subtopic we treated the plant as a body of vegetative organs: root, stem, leaf. Now the plant switches jobs entirely.
Look at the board, where a vegetative shoot stands beside a floral shoot. Same architecture, different programme running on it.
When a flowering plant is ready to reproduce, its shoot tip stops making leaves and starts making a flower instead.

And that single sentence is the key to this whole subtopic. A flower is nothing more than a modified shoot whose growing tip has been reprogrammed to produce floral parts at its nodes, rather than ordinary leaves.
Now take the consequence, because it explains what a flower looks like. In a floral shoot the internodes do not elongate. They stay squeezed to nearly nothing.
So all those parts sit crowded together on a compressed axis. That is exactly why a flower looks like a tight rosette rather than a long stalk with things spaced out along it.
The swollen tip of that compressed axis has a name you will use constantly: the thalamus. Every whorl of the flower is borne on it.
<curious>So hold this frame for the rest of the subtopic. Every floral part you are about to name is sitting in a position where a leaf could have been. The flower is a shoot that changed its mind.
पिछले subtopic में हमने plant को vegetative organs का body माना था — root, stem, leaf। अब plant अपना काम पूरी तरह बदल देता है।
Board देखिए, जहाँ एक vegetative shoot के बग़ल में एक floral shoot खड़ा है। Architecture वही, पर उस पर चल रहा programme अलग।
जब कोई flowering plant reproduce करने के लिए तैयार होता है, तो उसका shoot tip leaves बनाना बंद कर देता है और उसकी जगह flower बनाना शुरू कर देता है।
और यही एक sentence इस पूरे subtopic की चाबी है। Flower इससे ज़्यादा कुछ नहीं — एक modified shoot, जिसका growing tip reprogram हो चुका है कि वो अपने nodes पर ordinary leaves नहीं, floral parts बनाए।
अब इसका नतीजा पकड़िए, क्योंकि यही बताता है कि flower दिखता कैसा है। Floral shoot में internodes elongate होते ही नहीं। वो लगभग शून्य तक सिमटे रहते हैं।
इसलिए सारे parts एक compressed axis पर ठुँसे हुए बैठते हैं। यही वजह है कि flower एक कसा हुआ rosette लगता है, न कि लंबा stalk जिस पर चीज़ें दूर-दूर लगी हों।
उस compressed axis के फूले हुए tip का नाम आप बार-बार इस्तेमाल करेंगे — thalamus। Flower का हर whorl इसी पर बैठा होता है।
<curious>तो बाक़ी subtopic के लिए यही frame पकड़े रहिए। आप जिस भी floral part का नाम लेने वाले हैं, वो उस जगह बैठा है जहाँ एक leaf हो सकती थी। Flower वो shoot है जिसने अपना इरादा बदल दिया।

board_events.text: A plant that produced one flower at the very tip of its main stem would be done after one bloom.
So most plants spread their flowers along a branch system called the inflorescence.
Inflorescence: the arrangement of flowers on the floral axis.
The point of it: put out more flowers, and present them well for pollinators.
A solitary flower is a single flower borne alone.
Before you describe a single flower, ask how the plant deploys its flowers at all.

segments.text: Before we go anywhere near a single flower, there is a logistical question the plant has to solve first.
Look at the board, on the left. A plant that produced one flower at the very tip of its main stem would be done after one bloom.
The tip became a flower, so the tip cannot grow any more. One flower, one chance, one season. For most plants that is a poor bet.
So most plants spread their flowers along a branch system, and that branch system has a name: the inflorescence.
The definition is worth saying exactly, because it is a board favourite. An inflorescence is the arrangement of flowers on the floral axis. It is an arrangement, not an organ.
And the whole point of an inflorescence is twofold: to put out more flowers, and to present them well for pollinators. Quantity and display, at once.
The exception has a name too. A solitary flower is a single flower borne alone, not as part of a branch system.
<curious>So the order of thought for this subtopic is settled. First ask how the plant deploys its flowers. Only then zoom into one of them and start naming parts.
किसी एक flower के पास जाने से पहले, plant को एक logistical सवाल हल करना पड़ता है।
Board देखिए, बाईं तरफ़। जो plant अपने main stem के बिल्कुल tip पर एक flower बना दे, वो एक bloom के बाद ख़त्म।
Tip flower बन गया, तो अब tip बढ़ ही नहीं सकता। एक flower, एक मौक़ा, एक season। ज़्यादातर plants के लिए ये घाटे का सौदा है।
इसलिए ज़्यादातर plants अपने flowers को एक branch system पर फैलाते हैं, और उस branch system का नाम है inflorescence।
Definition बिल्कुल ठीक बोलिए, क्योंकि boards को ये पसंद है। Inflorescence यानी floral axis पर flowers की arrangement। ये एक arrangement है, कोई organ नहीं।
और inflorescence का पूरा मक़सद दो हिस्सों में है — ज़्यादा flowers निकालना, और उन्हें pollinators के सामने अच्छे से पेश करना। Quantity और display, एक साथ।
Exception का भी नाम है। Solitary flower यानी अकेला लगा हुआ एक flower, किसी branch system का हिस्सा नहीं।
<curious>तो इस subtopic के सोचने का क्रम तय हो गया। पहले पूछिए कि plant अपने flowers कैसे तैनात करता है। उसके बाद ही किसी एक में zoom करके parts के नाम लीजिए।

board_events.text: Racemose: the main axis keeps growing indefinitely and bears flowers along its sides.
Oldest flowers at the bottom, youngest near the growing tip. This bottom-to-top order is ACROPETAL. Example: Brassica, mustard.
Cymose: the main axis stops, because its tip itself becomes a flower.
Further flowers arise below it, so the oldest flower is at the top. This is BASIPETAL order. Example: Solanum.
At a glance: find the tip. A flower sitting at the very tip means cymose. A free growing point means racemose.
Racemose axis keeps growing (acropetal); cymose axis stops at a terminal flower (basipetal).

segments.text: There are two great strategies for building an inflorescence, and they differ in exactly one decision: does the main axis keep growing, or does it stop by turning into a flower?
Look at the board and take them side by side, because that one decision drives everything else that follows.
In a racemose inflorescence the main axis keeps growing indefinitely and bears flowers along its sides. The tip stays a growing point, and it never commits.
So the oldest flowers are at the bottom, opened long ago, and the youngest are near the growing tip. That bottom-to-top order is called acropetal, and the example is Brassica, the mustard.
In a cymose inflorescence the main axis stops, and it stops for a definite reason: its tip itself becomes a flower. The growing point is spent.
Further flowers then arise below it, so the oldest flower is the one at the top. That is basipetal order, and the example is Solanum.

Think about it this way. A racemose axis is an escalator that never stops, rising and dropping off flowers along the way, newest near the top. A cymose axis is a staircase that ends in a locked door: the topmost step was built first and blocks any further climb, so building continues downward.

<whisper>So the at-a-glance routine is one move. Find the tip of the main axis. A flower sitting at the very tip means cymose, youngest below. A free growing point with flowers along the sides means racemose, youngest at the top.
Inflorescence बनाने की दो बड़ी strategies हैं, और उनमें फ़र्क़ ठीक एक decision का है — main axis बढ़ता रहता है, या flower बनकर रुक जाता है?
Board देखिए और दोनों को साथ-साथ लीजिए, क्योंकि वही एक decision आगे का सब कुछ तय करता है।
Racemose inflorescence में main axis indefinitely बढ़ता रहता है और अपनी sides पर flowers लगाता जाता है। Tip growing point ही बना रहता है, कभी commit नहीं करता।
इसलिए सबसे पुराने flowers नीचे होते हैं, जो बहुत पहले खिले थे, और सबसे नए growing tip के पास। इस नीचे-से-ऊपर वाले order को कहते हैं acropetal, और example है Brassica, यानी mustard।
Cymose inflorescence में main axis रुक जाता है, और एक तय वजह से रुकता है — उसका tip ख़ुद ही flower बन जाता है। Growing point ख़र्च हो गया।
फिर बाक़ी flowers उसके नीचे से निकलते हैं, तो सबसे पुराना flower सबसे ऊपर वाला होता है। यही basipetal order है, और example है Solanum।

इसे ऐसे सोचिए। Racemose axis वो escalator है जो कभी रुकता नहीं — ऊपर उठता जाता है और रास्ते में flowers छोड़ता जाता है, सबसे नए ऊपर के पास। Cymose axis वो सीढ़ी है जो बंद दरवाज़े पर ख़त्म होती है — सबसे ऊपर वाली सीढ़ी पहले बनी और आगे चढ़ना रोक दिया, तो निर्माण नीचे की तरफ़ चलता रहा।

<whisper>तो at-a-glance routine एक ही move है। Main axis का tip ढूँढिए। बिल्कुल tip पर flower बैठा है तो cymose, सबसे नए नीचे। Tip पर खुला growing point और sides पर flowers हैं तो racemose, सबसे नए ऊपर।

board_events.text: Pedicel: the flower stalk.
Bract: a reduced leaf at the base of the pedicel.
A flower with a bract is bracteate; without one, ebracteate.
A solitary flower is a single flower borne alone. It may be axillary, sitting in a leaf axil.
The bract is a leaf, reduced. Another reminder that a flower is a shoot.
These three terms open every semi-technical description you will write later.

segments.text: Three small terms now, and they look trivial until you meet them as the opening line of a five-mark description.
Look at the board. The stalk that carries the flower is the pedicel. That is all it means: the flower stalk.
At the base of the pedicel there may be a bract, and a bract is a reduced leaf. Not a petal, not a sepal. A leaf that has been scaled down.
So the flower gets described by whether it has one. A flower with a bract is bracteate. A flower without one is ebracteate, and that little e at the front means without.
And we can now finish the definition we started earlier. A solitary flower is a single flower borne alone, rather than in a branch system. It is often axillary, sitting in the axil of a leaf.
Now notice what the bract quietly proves. It is a leaf, reduced. It is sitting exactly where a leaf would sit on any shoot.
That is your reminder, arriving from a second direction, that a flower is a shoot. The plant did not invent new organs for reproduction. It repurposed the ones it had.
These three terms feel small now, but hold on to them. Bracteate or ebracteate is the first field of every semi-technical description you will write in the last subtopic of this chapter.
अब तीन छोटे terms, और ये तब तक मामूली लगते हैं जब तक ये पाँच-marks वाली description की पहली line बनकर सामने न आ जाएँ।
Board देखिए। जो stalk flower को उठाए हुए है, वो है pedicel। बस इतना ही मतलब — flower का डंठल।
Pedicel के base पर एक bract हो सकता है, और bract एक reduced leaf है। न petal, न sepal। एक leaf, जिसे छोटा कर दिया गया।
तो flower का description इसी से बनता है कि उसके पास ये है या नहीं। Bract वाला flower bracteate है। बिना bract वाला ebracteate, और आगे लगा वो छोटा सा e का मतलब है — बिना।
और अब हम वो definition पूरी कर सकते हैं जो पहले शुरू की थी। Solitary flower यानी अकेला लगा एक flower, किसी branch system में नहीं। ये अक्सर axillary होता है, यानी leaf के axil में बैठा हुआ।
अब ध्यान दीजिए कि bract चुपचाप क्या साबित कर रहा है। ये एक leaf है, reduced। और ये ठीक वहीं बैठा है जहाँ किसी भी shoot पर leaf बैठती।
यही आपका reminder है, दूसरी दिशा से आता हुआ — flower एक shoot है। Plant ने reproduction के लिए नए organs ईजाद नहीं किए। जो पास थे, उन्हीं को नया काम दे दिया।
ये तीनों terms अभी छोटे लगते हैं, पर पकड़े रखिए। Bracteate या ebracteate हर semi-technical description का पहला field है, जो आप इस chapter के आख़िरी subtopic में लिखेंगे।

board_events.text: A typical flower carries up to four whorls of parts, attached to a swollen receptacle called the thalamus.
From outside in: calyx (sepals, usually green, protective), then corolla (petals, often coloured, attract pollinators).
Then androecium (stamens, the male parts), then gynoecium (carpels, the female parts).
Calyx and corolla are the ACCESSORY, non-essential whorls. Androecium and gynoecium are the ESSENTIAL, reproductive whorls.
A flower with both essential whorls is bisexual; with only one, unisexual.
When calyx and corolla are not distinguishable, as in lily, the whorl is the perianth and its units are tepals.

segments.text: Now zoom into a single flower, and take the parts in the order the plant built them: from outside in.
A typical flower carries up to four whorls of parts, all attached to that swollen receptacle we named, the thalamus. Look at the board and read from the outside.
First the calyx, whose units are sepals. They are usually green and their job is protective: they wrap the bud before it opens.
Then the corolla, whose units are petals. Often coloured, and their job is to attract pollinators. Everything you find beautiful about a flower is advertising.
Then the androecium, the stamens, which are the male parts. And innermost, the gynoecium, the carpels, which are the female parts.
Now the division that questions are built on. Calyx and corolla are the accessory or non-essential whorls. Androecium and gynoecium are the essential, reproductive whorls.
And that division gives you the sex terms directly. A flower with both essential whorls is bisexual. A flower with only one of them is unisexual.

One more case to hold. When calyx and corolla are not distinguishable, as in lily, the undifferentiated whorl is called the perianth, and its units are tepals. Remember that name. It walks straight into the family questions later.
अब किसी एक flower में zoom कीजिए, और parts को उसी क्रम में लीजिए जिसमें plant ने उन्हें बनाया — बाहर से अंदर।
एक typical flower में parts के चार तक whorls होते हैं, और सब उसी फूले हुए receptacle से जुड़े होते हैं जिसका नाम हमने लिया — thalamus। Board देखिए और बाहर से पढ़िए।
पहले calyx, जिसकी units हैं sepals। ये आम तौर पर green होते हैं और इनका काम protective है — खिलने से पहले ये bud को लपेटे रखते हैं।
फिर corolla, जिसकी units हैं petals। अक्सर coloured, और इनका काम है pollinators को attract करना। Flower में आपको जो कुछ भी सुंदर लगता है, वो असल में advertising है।
फिर androecium, यानी stamens, जो male parts हैं। और सबसे अंदर gynoecium, यानी carpels, जो female parts हैं।
अब वो बँटवारा जिस पर questions खड़े होते हैं। Calyx और corolla accessory यानी non-essential whorls हैं। Androecium और gynoecium essential यानी reproductive whorls हैं।
और यही बँटवारा sex के terms सीधे दे देता है। जिस flower में दोनों essential whorls हों, वो bisexual। जिसमें सिर्फ़ एक हो, वो unisexual।

एक case और पकड़ लीजिए। जब calyx और corolla अलग पहचाने ही न जाएँ, जैसे lily में, तो उस undifferentiated whorl को कहते हैं perianth, और उसकी units हैं tepals। ये नाम याद रखिए। ये आगे family वाले questions में सीधे चला आता है।

board_events.text: Limit one: this is still morphology, external form and arrangement.
Pollination, fertilisation and embryo development belong to a separate later chapter. Importing them here is a classic confusion.
Limit two: 'non-essential' does not mean useless.
Sepals protect the bud and petals recruit pollinators. The word only means 'not directly reproductive'.
Limit three: several distinctions here are pairs students reflexively swap.
Symmetry, aestivation classes, racemose versus cymose. Always anchor each term to its standard example.

segments.text: Three limits now, exactly as we did in the last subtopic, because this material has its own way of going wrong.
Look at the board. Limit one: this is still morphology. External form and arrangement, the things you can see and count.

The detailed events of reproduction, pollination, fertilisation, embryo development, belong to a separate later chapter. Importing them here is a classic confusion, and the marks go to whoever stayed in scope.
So if you catch yourself writing about how the pollen reaches the ovule, stop. You were asked what the flower looks like, not how it works.
Limit two is a word that misleads honest students. Non-essential does not mean useless.

Sepals protect the bud through its whole vulnerable stage, and petals recruit pollinators, without which nothing happens at all. The word only means not directly reproductive. It is a job title, not a judgement.
Limit three is about how this topic is examined. Several distinctions here are pairs that students reflexively swap.

<curious>Symmetry, the aestivation classes, racemose versus cymose. Notice they are all pairs or short lists of look-alike names. So always anchor each term to its standard plant, and the swap has nowhere to happen.
अब तीन limits, ठीक वैसे ही जैसे पिछले subtopic में की थीं, क्योंकि ये material अपने ही तरीक़े से ग़लत होता है।
Board देखिए। Limit one — ये अब भी morphology है। External form और arrangement, यानी वो चीज़ें जो दिखती हैं और गिनी जा सकती हैं।

Reproduction की detailed घटनाएँ — pollination, fertilisation, embryo development — किसी अलग, बाद वाले chapter की हैं। उन्हें यहाँ घसीट लाना classic confusion है, और marks उसे मिलते हैं जो scope में रहा।
तो अगर आप ख़ुद को ये लिखते पकड़ें कि pollen ovule तक कैसे पहुँचता है, रुक जाइए। पूछा गया था flower दिखता कैसा है, ये नहीं कि काम कैसे करता है।
Limit two एक ऐसा शब्द है जो ईमानदार students को भी भटका देता है। Non-essential का मतलब बेकार नहीं है।

Sepals पूरे नाज़ुक दौर में bud की हिफ़ाज़त करते हैं, और petals pollinators को बुलाते हैं, जिनके बिना कुछ होता ही नहीं। इस शब्द का मतलब सिर्फ़ इतना है — directly reproductive नहीं। ये job title है, कोई फ़ैसला नहीं।
Limit three इस बात की है कि ये topic पूछा कैसे जाता है। यहाँ कई distinctions ऐसी जोड़ियाँ हैं जिन्हें students आदतन उलट देते हैं।

<curious>Symmetry, aestivation की classes, racemose बनाम cymose। ध्यान दीजिए, ये सब जोड़ियाँ हैं या मिलते-जुलते नामों की छोटी lists। तो हर term को उसके standard plant से बाँध दीजिए, फिर उलटने की जगह ही नहीं बचेगी।
